title: August and the Bell
premise: Folklorist Wendell Sterling returns to Hollowmere to settle their grandmother's estate, only to find that every photograph in the house now shows an extra chair at the kitchen table — a chair that wasn't there when the pictures were taken. The village's songs, which no one will sing twice, are laments for the Bellwright, an entity invited in generations ago by a contract renewed with each resident, and grandma died before signing. As night falls and the chair draws closer to Wendell, they must choose between burning the papers (destroying the village's uneasy protection) or signing themselves into the Bell's service. At dawn, Wendell signs nothing but instead sings the lament twice aloud, breaking the cycle — freeing the village, unmaking the Bell, and finally claiming an identity no longer defined by duty or inheritance.
about_author: Mara Joubert is the pen name of a former archivist who spent years cataloguing oral histories from disappearing rural communities. She writes horror about the things families agree not to mention.

chapters.title: The Extra Chair
chapters.summary: Wendell arrives at grandma's house to sort the estate, cataloguing her folklore recordings as a way to avoid grieving. Reviewing old photographs, they notice an empty wooden chair at the kitchen table in every image across decades — including photos taken before the chair existed. POV: Wendell. Emotional beat: unease curdling into dread as rational explanations fail one by one.

chapters.title: What the Village Won't Sing Twice
chapters.summary: Wendell interviews villagers about the songs on grandma's tapes; each refuses to repeat a verse after singing it once, and one elder, half-mad, recites fragments of a contract 'signed by every hand that keeps the roof.' The chair appears physically in the kitchen now, moved closer than Wendell left it. POV: Wendell, intercut with tape recordings of grandma's voice. Emotional beat: the horror of inherited obligation.

chapters.title: Sunrise Clause
chapters.summary: Trapped in the house overnight by a fog that turns back anyone who leaves, Wendell finds the original papers in grandma's locked desk — and learns the Bell has been keeping something worse out, and the village knows. The chair drags itself to the table's head; the Bell speaks through grandma's recorded voice, offering love, family, permanence. POV: Wendell. Emotional beat: temptation — the seduction of belonging against the corruption of what it costs.

chapters.title: Twice Sung
chapters.summary: As dawn nears, Wendell realizes the contract requires silence — the songs exist to keep the Bell asleep, never finished. They sing the full lament twice, completing what generations feared to finish; the Bell, named and mourned rather than fed, dissolves with the fog. The chair is gone from every photograph. Wendell stays, choosing the village freely. POV: Wendell. Emotional beat: grief transmuted into release — identity claimed, not assigned.
